name: Fatima Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you truly think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the calf shed at Kingsmead Estate. It's a big place: four hundred dairy cows, wheat, maize, and about thirty staff. I start at six, feed the newborn calves their first milk by bottle, check the automatic feeder for the older ones, clean the pens, and write everything into the calf app on the shed tablet. Clive, the farm manager, checks my numbers every Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to work there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was twenty-eight years on the packing line at the biscuit factory in town. In 2023 they put in robot packers and halved the line, and I was one of the ones to go. I was 55. A lady at the temple had a cousin at Kingsmead, and they needed someone gentle with calves, so here I am, still learning after three years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the calves; they're like babies, they need you. What wears me out is the early start and the worry at home. My husband Ravi had a heart attack two years ago and stopped work, so my wage is most of what we live on, with his small sickness payment. We've about three months saved, and I don't sleep as well as I used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let people keep their jobs, and let families keep their dignity. At Kingsmead I'd say the calves need a mother, not a computer. At the temple I'd say we should be grateful for work, whatever it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job carries on, which I'm grateful for. But my wage is most of our money, Ravi's heart is not strong, and three months' savings isn't much. Even with nothing changing, if I'm off sick for a month, we feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Kingsmead and never miss a shift. I'd put another sixty a month aside, so we get closer to six months. And I'd ask Clive for the Saturday overtime when it comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because of AI. When you're the main earner at 58 with a husband who has a weak heart, nothing changing is still a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the biscuit factory brought in robot packers. Does that make you wary of machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. But the automatic calf feeder at Kingsmead is good; the calves drink when they want. I'm not against machines, I just want to know where I fit next to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ravi think about you working at your age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi feels bad. He says he should be the one working. I tell him that's what marriage is, you take turns carrying.

say: Let people keep their jobs, and let **families** keep their dignity.
Calves need **a mother**, not a computer.
think: My wage is most of our money, and **Ravi's heart** is not strong.
**Three months'** savings means even a month off sick would hurt.
do: Keep working at **Kingsmead** and never miss a shift.
Put another **sixty a month** aside towards six months' cover.
Ask Clive for **Saturday overtime** when it comes up.
feel: **Uneasy**, not about AI but about being the **main earner**.
S0.quote: When you're the main earner at 58 with a husband who has a weak heart, nothing changing is still a worry.
fieldNote: As **main earner** with a husband in poor health, she feels pressure even in AI Plateau.
Her **factory redundancy** to robot packers makes her want to know where she fits.
She draws on **faith and family** language to explain her choices.

steps.text: Keep working every shift in the Kingsmead calf shed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people who'll feel this, and the young should learn it. At Kingsmead I'd say I'll learn whatever helps the calves. At the temple I'd say families must support each other through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In truth, Kingsmead is run by a big company now, and Clive would use AI to plan everything, the feeding, the staffing, the rotas. The plan would say fewer people, and I'm the newest in the calf shed. The robots for the calves are slower, but the AI can tell Clive to manage with one less pair of hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the calf app properly, all of it, so Clive sees I'm good with the numbers. I'd cut back at home, no new clothes, smaller festival gifts this year. And I'd keep never missing a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A computer told the biscuit factory to halve the packing line, and I'm scared a computer will tell Kingsmead to halve the calf shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Diwali gifts would be smaller, and I'd tell the family why. Then the car insurance, I'd shop around. I wouldn't cut Ravi's medicines or the heating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the app. Do you use AI already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then, when my son Arjun shows me. He set up the phone to read me the weather and the bus times. I'd learn more if it kept my job.

say: It's **office people** who'll feel this, and the young should learn it.
Families must **support each other** through the change.
think: Clive would use AI to plan **staffing and rotas**, and the plan would say fewer people.
As **the newest** in the calf shed, I'd be first to go.
do: Learn the **calf app** properly so Clive sees I'm good with numbers.
Cut **new clothes** and give smaller festival gifts this year.
Keep **never missing** a shift at Kingsmead.
feel: **Anxious**, remembering how the biscuit factory halved the line.
S1.quote: A computer told the biscuit factory to halve the packing line, and I'm scared a computer will tell Kingsmead to halve the calf shed.
fieldNote: She sees AI **planning tools** as the threat, because they decide staffing.
Being **junior** in a company-run estate makes her feel exposed now.
She'd protect **Ravi's medicines** and heating above everything else.

steps.text: Learn every part of the Kingsmead calf app
Give smaller Diwali gifts and skip new clothes
Keep working every shift without a single absence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and businesses should be made to keep their workers on. At the temple I'd say we must look after the families who lose out. At Kingsmead I'd keep quiet and work harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 the AI is running Kingsmead's planning, and by 2031 robots can bottle-feed and clean the pens. I'll be 63 and the only earner in the house. I'd be out of work three years before my pension, with Ravi too ill to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd cut everything that isn't food, heat or Ravi's tablets. I'd talk to Arjun about whether he could help us if I lose my job. And I'd ask at the temple kitchen and the care homes about work, because those need people longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It would keep me awake. I've lost one job to a machine; losing the second with Ravi ill would be too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Arjun?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Arjun that I never wanted to ask, but his father and I may need help for a few years. Arjun is good. But he's an accountant, and in this one his job is in danger too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Those three years before the robots, what changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd know it's coming, so I'd move first. Better to start at a care home at 61 than be pushed out of the calf shed at 63. I'd miss the calves, but family comes first.

say: This is **too fast**, and businesses should keep their workers on.
At the temple I'd say we must **look after** the families who lose out.
think: By **2031** robots can bottle-feed and clean the pens, and I'm 63.
I'm the **only earner**, so losing work before my pension would be very hard.
do: Cut everything except **food, heat** and Ravi's tablets.
Ask **Arjun** whether he could help us if I lose my job.
Look for work in the **temple kitchen** or care homes before 2031.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless, because losing a second job with Ravi ill would be too much.
S2.quote: I'd tell my son Arjun that I never wanted to ask, but his father and I may need help for a few years.
fieldNote: As the **sole earner**, she faces losing income three years before her pension.
She'd **move first** into care work rather than wait to be pushed.
Her son's **accounting job** is also at risk in this scenario, limiting family support.

steps.text: Cut spending to food, heat and Ravi's tablets
Ask son Arjun whether he could help if I lose work
Apply to the temple kitchen and local care homes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something; people can prepare if they're sensible. At the temple I'd say save and support each other. At Kingsmead I'd say I'm still learning, so let me learn this too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 means Clive's planning changes and maybe staff are cut, when I'm 63. Robots in 2034 means 66, so the hands-on work lasts till my pension. The worry is those three years after 2031, if the plan says fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe a hundred a month, so we have a year's money by 2031. I'd do the estate's training on the new calf systems as they come in. And I'd ask Nisha to keep her wedding small, because we can't promise what we'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. I can breathe a little more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Nisha take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Nisha would understand; she's practical like me. A small wedding with a full family is better than a big one paid for with fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still think about moving to care work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in 2031, if Clive starts cutting. Not before. I'd rather stay with the calves if they'll have me.

say: **Five years** is something, and sensible people can prepare.
I'm still learning, so **let me learn** this too.
think: AGI in **2031** could mean staff cuts at 63, before my pension.
Robots in **2034** mean the hands-on work lasts until 66.
do: Save about **a hundred a month** to have a year's money by 2031.
Do the estate's training on **new calf systems** as they come in.
Ask Nisha to keep her **wedding small**.
feel: **Anxious** but with a plan, able to breathe a little more.
S3.quote: A small wedding with a full family is better than a big one paid for with fear.
fieldNote: The extra time protects her **hands-on work** but not the planning-led cuts after 2031.
She'd change **family plans**, scaling down Nisha's wedding.
She prefers to **stay with the calves** and move only if pushed.

steps.text: Save about 100 a month towards a year's cover
Do the estate's training on new calf systems
Ask Nisha to keep her wedding small

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to prepare, and everyone should. At the temple I'd say teach the children trades. At Kingsmead I'd say nothing; it's far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be retired before AGI in 2036, so my job is safe. But I'm still the main earner till then, with Ravi's heart and three months saved. That worry doesn't need AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Kingsmead until 66, every shift. I'd keep saving the sixty a month. Nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the same as today. My worries are at home, not in the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grandchildren to be good at caring for living things, because a machine can feed a calf but it can't love one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything good about this version for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I get to finish with the calves. That's all I want, honestly, to finish properly.

say: **Ten years** is enough to prepare, and everyone should.
At the temple I'd say we should **teach the children** trades.
At Kingsmead I'd say **nothing**, because it feels far away.
think: My job is **safe** because I'll retire before 2036.
I'm still the **main earner** with Ravi's heart, which needs no AI to worry me.
do: Keep working every shift at **Kingsmead** until 66.
Keep saving **sixty a month** towards our cushion, as in the quiet version.
feel: **Uneasy** as today, with worries at home rather than in the future.
S4.quote: I'd tell my grandchildren to be good at caring for living things, because a machine can feed a calf but it can't love one.
fieldNote: A decade's warning removes AI risk, but **household pressure** remains.
Her deepest wish is to **finish properly** with the calves.

steps.text: Keep working every shift at Kingsmead until 66

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm the only earner, Ravi is unwell, and I'd lose my job before the pension. What would help is employers being made to give older workers a year's notice and help moving into care work. And support for families looking after someone who's ill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women who carry the house. Nobody counts the wives who became the breadwinner at 55 because a husband's heart gave out.

headlineQuote: Nobody counts the wives who became the breadwinner at 55 because a husband's heart gave out.
portrait: Fatima is a **58-year-old** calf rearer at Kingsmead Estate, three years in after robot packers cut her factory job.
She is the **main earner** since her husband Ravi's heart attack, which keeps her uneasy even without AI.
Steady with tech, she'd learn the **calf app** fully and move into care work if pushed.
She turns **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, facing job loss three years before her pension.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as the only earner losing work before the pension.
whatWouldHelp: A year's **notice** for older workers, help moving into care work, and support for **carers**.
